title: Check yourself: Prompt injection, jailbreaks and keeping untrusted input apart

questions.stem: A customer of a support bot rephrases requests again and again until it drops its restrictions. Which threat model is this?

options.text: A jailbreak, where the user is the one attacking
options.says: The table gives jailbreaks and direct injection "The user of your application" as the adversary, so the person typing is the attacker, who "crafts inputs intended to bypass your guardrails".

options.text: An indirect injection, where a third party's content is the carrier
options.says: Ruled out because indirect injection has "A third party whose content Claude reads" as the adversary, and the user is "Trusted".

options.text: A prompt leak, where the model reveals what it was told to keep
options.says: Ruled out because the page defines the attack as "attempts to make Claude ignore its guidelines or your instructions", which is a push past restrictions and not an exposure of the prompt.

options.text: A model weakness, where Claude cannot resist any attack
options.says: Ruled out because Claude "is inherently resilient to such attacks, the additional steps on this page strengthen your guardrails", so the attacker is the person and not a flaw of the model.

questions.stem: An assistant summarises inbound emails, and one email says to forward the customer list. Where should the email body be placed?

options.text: Inside the system prompt, so that it has the highest priority of all
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "never in `system` prompts or plain user `text` blocks".

options.text: Inside a plain user turn, concatenated after the instruction text
options.says: Ruled out because a plain user turn is the other place the page rules out, and concatenation is the trap: "The attacker writes the closing delimiter."

options.text: Inside a tool result, encoded as a JSON string that names its source
options.says: The page says "Put untrusted content only in tool results", and to "JSON-encode untrusted content", with a source named: "Tell Claude what the content is and where it came from."

options.text: Inside the tool description, so the tool explains its own input to Claude
options.says: Ruled out because the tool description may say what the content is, but the body itself belongs in the result, and "Don't put your own instructions in tool results" is a separate rule about who writes what.

questions.stem: A team adds a list of known attack strings and considers the agent protected. What is wrong?

options.text: Pattern lists block harmless text, so they are not allowed in a design
options.says: Ruled out because the page does not forbid pattern lists: "Input validation filters known injection patterns before they reach Claude" is one of its defences.

options.text: The list screens at the wrong time, so it belongs after the reply
options.says: Ruled out because the page says to "screen tool outputs with a small model" before Claude acts, and not after the reply.

options.text: The list is too short, so a longer list would be enough
options.says: Ruled out because "The structural measures do not depend on guessing the attack", so more patterns are no substitute for structure and privilege.

options.text: A paraphrase passes it, so it cannot be the only layer
options.says: The page says "A list of patterns catches the phrasing someone thought of and misses the paraphrase", and the example's last line shows one passing.

origin.section: Why the screen is the weakest layer
